Whether the supply is DC, which is more dangerous than AC at the same voltage

Current path through the body, magnitude, duration, and frequency (for AC)

explanation: Harm is caused by current flowing through the body. Its size depends on the voltage and the body's resistance (wet skin, contact area), and severity rises with a path across the chest, longer contact and AC at 50-60 Hz, which can cause ventricular fibrillation at currents of around 50 mA.

distractorExplanations.a: Voltage drives current, but severity depends on the current that flows, its path and duration, which depend on body resistance.
distractorExplanations.b: AC at 50-60 Hz is generally more dangerous than DC at the same voltage because it causes muscle tetany and fibrillation.
distractorExplanations.c: Fuses protect cables from overcurrent and blow at currents far above lethal body currents of around 50 mA; they do not prevent shock.

prompt: A site fits RCDs to the socket circuits that feed its portable tools. What do these devices primarily protect against?

Voltage surges from lightning strikes that could damage connected electronic equipment
Earth leakage currents that could cause electric shock and some fire risks
Short circuits between live and neutral conductors in the cable

explanation: An RCD compares the current in the live and neutral conductors; if current leaks to earth, for example through a person, the imbalance trips it quickly (a 30 mA device trips within about 40 ms at higher fault currents), limiting shock duration. distractorExplanations.a: Overcurrent protection is the role of fuses and MCBs; an RCD detects imbalance between live and neutral.
distractorExplanations.b: Surge protection devices handle transient overvoltages; RCDs respond to earth leakage current.
distractorExplanations.d: A live-neutral short creates no imbalance, so an RCD may not trip; fuses or MCBs clear short circuits.

prompt: When two departments blame each other after a near miss at a shared walkway, the investigation should?

Examine the shared interface, housekeeping, lighting, and rules rather than focusing only on individual fault
Interview the workers involved to establish who was at fault, then apply the disciplinary policy
Have each department investigate separately and submit its own report to the safety committee

explanation: Interface areas shared by departments often fail because nobody owns housekeeping, lighting or route rules. A joint investigation of the shared system finds those underlying causes, whereas assigning blame to one department or individual leaves the interface unchanged.

distractorExplanations.a: Ownership on a plan does not address interface failures; the investigation should look at shared systems.

distractorExplanations.d: Separate investigations repeat the blame split; a joint investigation of the interface is needed.
